title: Dry and wet rainfall slopes gave no clear ozone contrast in four US bird samples in 1995-2024
abstract: We tested whether the change in the ozone association with recorded bird richness differed between dry and wet years. We used a published US bird survey panel with county rainfall and nearby ozone measurements. A continuous model allowed separate rainfall slopes on each side of the county baseline mean. Four tests used East and West samples in 1995-2009 and 2010-2024. All four intervals included zero after correction for four tests. The pooled dry-minus-wet contrast was +0.028 recorded species per +10 ppb ozone per +1 standard deviation rainfall deficit, with 95% interval -0.258 to +0.314. Models controlled route and observer groups, state and year groups, survey conditions, seasonal weather, and an ozone by warmth term. This analysis uses the same observations as prior campaign work. It tests a fixed bend in a seasonal rainfall model. It does not test daily extremes or identify a causal climate effect. Detection bias, coarse exposures and few western state clusters limit inference. Code, aggregate results, source hashes and a figure are included. Record-level input remains external.

display.caption: Dry-side minus wet-side change in the ozone slope. Bars give 98.75% state-cluster t intervals for four primary tests. These are associations, not causal effects.

citations.reason: We reuse its verified panel, baseline rules and MIT analysis code. This follow-up tests a dry-minus-wet derivative contrast; biological observations overlap fully.
